relationships.label: Spectre Systems
relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey co-founded Spectre Systems with Michael Toth and Marion Nalepa. Bilbrey designed and programmed the games, Toth handled business arrangements and negotiated distribution through Esoterica, and Nalepa contributed sound to ICBM Attack.

relationships.label: Joining the DNA circle

participants.name: Jeff Frederiksen
participants.role: chipset designer, recruiter, and later employer

relationships.description: After Brett Bilbrey's reverse engineering exposed an intercept-register hardware problem, Jeff Frederiksen invited him to Chicago. Bilbrey remained at the University of Michigan and demonstrated his remote cartridge-development system by creating ICBM Attack and then Treasure Cove.

relationships.label: Brief overlap at Dave Nutting Associates
relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey recalled working briefly with Alan McNeil near the end of McNeil's time at Dave Nutting Associates. Bilbrey identified Dave Otto as the facility manager during the same period.

relationships.label: Action Graphics and Cosmic Raiders

participants.role: contract programmer assigned an early Defender-like version
Action Graphics head and released-game contributor

relationships.description: Dave Nutting and Jeff Frederiksen formed Action Graphics with Bob Ogdon, who served as president. The company contracted Brett Bilbrey after his two Spectre cartridges and supplied a DataMax UV-1 running TERSE. Bilbrey returned the system when the development method proved a poor fit; the released Cosmic Raiders was completed by Ogdon, Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting.

relationships.label: Technical publishing and user groups

participants.name: Fred Cornett
participants.role: Cursor editor and Peek & Poke Manual author

relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey shared reverse-engineering results, assembly routines, sprite techniques, and sound techniques through user groups and newsletters. He recalled teaching Fred Cornett material used in Cursor's Peek & Poke Manual and working with George Moses on several Bally Arcade projects.

relationships.label: From DNA to digital video
relationships.description: After DNA's game-development operation closed, Brett Bilbrey joined Jeff Frederiksen and David Shu at Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories. Their digital-video frame-buffer work became Video Explorer and led to the Intelligent Resources–Integrated Systems spin-off.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade ROM and early software

participants.name: Jeff McKenna
participants.role: consultant who completed Bingo Math near ship time

relationships.description: Alan McNeil worked with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp on the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM. McNeil also credited consultant Jeff McKenna with completing Bingo Math near ship time, while his own work included DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, the ROM's interrupt and sound routines, Sea Wolf II, and the original TERSE engine.

relationships.label: DNA's Z80 development system
relationships.description: Alan McNeil recalled replacing DNA's crowded ModComp and Mostek-assembler workflow with a dedicated Z80 system. Terry Coleman and Tony Miller designed much of the probe, Jim Hemmer handled schematics, layout, and wire-wrap, Dave Nutting built the cabinet, and Dave Otto assisted with wire-wrap and day-to-day facility work.

relationships.label: Office mates and TERSE

participants.role: DNA cartridge programmer and TERSE user

relationships.description: Rick Spiece shared an office with Alan McNeil at Dave Nutting Associates. Spiece remembered McNeil creating the original TERSE engine and later used the language to prototype cartridge work before completing released games in Z80 assembly.

relationships.label: From DNA to Stern and Xtar
relationships.description: After leaving DNA, Tony Miller helped staff Universal Research Laboratories for Stern and recruited Alan McNeil first, followed by former DNA colleagues Terry Coleman, Jim Hemmer, and Bill Jahnke. Miller managed Berzerk while McNeil designed and programmed the game; McNeil later created Frenzy and briefly joined Miller at Xtar to work on a 3D project.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on

participants.role: hardware design engineer and productization lead

relationships.description: Larry Leske began DNA's Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on before leaving for Zilog. Tony Miller then took over its hardware, brought the prototype toward a manufacturable design, and helped connect it to a dual Micropolis floppy drive. Miller handled setup and support during public demonstrations while Jay Fenton presented the software, which included Alan McNeil's TERSE language.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade hardware
relationships.description: Tony Miller worked at DNA while the Arcade's Address, Data, and I/O chips were being developed. He requested the BUZOFF signal so expansion hardware could isolate the custom-chip bus and return data to the Z80. Miller later described how Terry Coleman and Jeff Frederiksen verified the chip logic and how Jim Hemmer's printed-circuit work supported the console and later Stern team.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade games
relationships.description: Bob Ogdon's first DNA assignment became Brickyard/Clowns, with Scot L. Norris contributing audio. Ogdon and Rick Spiece co-developed Football, and Ogdon later designed and programmed Bally Pin with Norris again handling its sound.

relationships.label: Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor
relationships.description: After his home-cartridge work, Bob Ogdon moved to the coin-operated Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor projects. Ogdon credited Dave Nutting with the central ideas behind Gorf and Wizard of Wor, while later recollections identify Jay Fenton and other DNA specialists as members of the collaborative development group.

relationships.label: Coin-op designs brought home
relationships.description: Bob Ogdon adapted DNA's arcade work for the revived Astrocade as Space Fortress and The Incredible Wizard. As president of Action Graphics, he also supervised Dave Armstrong's first cartridge project, Quest for the Orb, using the studio's graphics-oriented development language.

people.name: Alan McNeil
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates programmer, creator of TERSE, and contributor to the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM and early software.
people.astrocadeSummary: Alan McNeil worked at Dave Nutting Associates from March 1977 through April 1979. He helped build the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp, while consultant Jeff McKenna joined near ship time to finish Bingo Math. McNeil's credited console work also includes DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, and the system ROM's interrupt and sound routines. For coin-operated hardware he wrote Sea Wolf II largely in TERSE, the compact, FORTH-derived Z80 language he created for DNA. McNeil recalled that TERSE removed a layer of indirection from FORTH's inner loop and used 1 KB disk blocks rather than a conventional file system.
people.laterCareerSummary: Tony Miller recruited McNeil from DNA as Universal Research Laboratories staffed the Stern group that created Berzerk. McNeil designed and programmed Berzerk and later Frenzy; former DNA coworkers Terry Coleman and Jim Hemmer handled hardware and printed-circuit work. McNeil later joined Miller at Xtar for a time to work on a 3D game.
accomplishments: Created TERSE, the Z80 stack language used for Sea Wolf II and later DNA games.
Worked with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp on the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM and wrote its interrupt and sound routines.
Programmed DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, and much of Sea Wolf II; consultant Jeff McKenna completed Bingo Math near the console's ship date.
Helped replace DNA's shared ModComp-based workflow with a dedicated Z80 development system built around 8-inch disks and later CP/M experiments.
Designed and programmed Stern's Berzerk and Frenzy after leaving DNA.

people.name: Bob Ogdon
people.astrocadeRole: Game designer and programmer at Dave Nutting Associates, leader of a DNA development team, and president of Action Graphics.
people.astrocadeSummary: Bob Ogdon entered game development after his wife, Julie, introduced him to Dave Nutting. A psychology graduate of the University of Puget Sound, he moved to Chicago and joined the group developing software for the Bally Professional Arcade. His first assignment became Brickyard/Clowns, including the home translation of Exidy's Clowns. He went on to co-develop Football with Rick Spiece and to design and program Bally Pin. DNA then moved him into coin-operated work on Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor. Contemporary accounts describe those games as team efforts: Ogdon shaped designs and led developers rather than producing every part alone.
people.laterCareerSummary: When Bally withdrew from the home-console market, Ogdon became president of Action Graphics, formed with Dave Nutting and Jeff Frederiksen to continue Astrocade cartridge development. The company produced later work including Cosmic Raiders, credited in the archive to Ogdon, Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting. Ogdon also supervised Dave Armstrong's first project, Quest for the Orb, using DNA's graphics-oriented development language.
accomplishments: Programmed Brickyard/Clowns, with Scot Norris supplying the audio; Clowns was the system's first 4 KB cartridge.
Co-developed Football with Rick Spiece and introduced horizontal scrolling to create a larger playing field.
Designed and programmed the two-playfield Bally Pin, again working with Scot Norris on audio.
Contributed game design and team leadership to Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor under Dave Nutting.
Adapted DNA coin-operated designs for the home system as Space Fortress and The Incredible Wizard.
Served as president of Action Graphics and contributed to Cosmic Raiders with Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting.
Supervised Dave Armstrong's development of Quest for the Orb.

people.name: Brett Bilbrey
people.astrocadeRole: Spectre Systems co-founder, Bally Arcade programmer and hardware designer, and later Action Graphics contract developer.
people.astrocadeSummary: While studying electrical engineering at the University of Michigan, Bilbrey bought a Bally Arcade, reverse-engineered its Z80-based hardware and ROM, and helped Spectre Systems build a TRS-80 development system that mapped expansion RAM into the console's cartridge space. His investigation of the intercept register and experiments with a light pen brought him into contact with Jeff Frederiksen, who invited him to Dave Nutting Associates. Bilbrey remained in school and used Spectre's tools to create ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove. He also designed and built the Spectre Systems controller used by ICBM Attack and intended for other games.
people.laterCareerSummary: After graduating, Bilbrey joined Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories after Bally's game-development operation at Dave Nutting Associates had closed. He later worked at Intelligent Resources–Integrated Systems and Intelligent Paradigm on computer and broadcast-video technology, including the Video Explorer frame buffer. He subsequently spent twelve years at Apple, where he led the Technology Advancement Group and worked on products and technologies including the Mac mini, Apple TV, and built-in iSight cameras.
accomplishments: Co-founded Spectre Systems with friends Michael Toth and Marion Nalepa; Toth handled business arrangements and Nalepa contributed sound to ICBM Attack.
Designed and programmed ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove using Spectre's custom Z80 development system.
Designed and built the Spectre Systems controller, combining an analog joystick, keypad, and side buttons for ICBM Attack and possible future games.
Published Bally Arcade assembly techniques and programs through The Arcadian and Cursor and shared discoveries with the Michigan Bally Users Group.
Preserved and shared source code, development notes, prototypes, tapes, and other early Bally Arcade material with the modern archive community.

Accepted an Action Graphics assignment for a Defender-like cartridge later released as Cosmic Raiders, but returned the UV-1 system after difficulty adapting to TERSE; he did not program the released game.

people.name: Tony Miller
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates hardware design engineer, Bally Professional Arcade add-on developer, and later manager of the Universal Research Laboratories team behind Stern's Berzerk.
people.astrocadeSummary: Tony Miller worked at Dave Nutting Associates while the Bally Professional Arcade and its three custom chips were being developed. His principal console project was the computer add-on planned to turn the Arcade into a fuller home computer. After Larry Leske left for Zilog, Miller took over the hardware, brought the prototype toward a product design, and helped interface it to a dual Micropolis floppy drive. Miller and Jay Fenton supported the machine at a late-1970s Winter CES and on a distributor tour through Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Seattle. The archive contains conflicting retrospective dates for those demonstrations and Miller's departure, so this profile keeps the chronology approximate.
people.laterCareerSummary: After leaving DNA for another coin-operated-game company, Miller helped staff Universal Research Laboratories for Stern. He recruited Alan McNeil first, followed by former DNA colleagues Terry Coleman, Jim Hemmer, and Bill Jahnke, and managed development of Berzerk. Miller later helped start Xtar, where McNeil briefly worked on a 3D game. In the Bally Alley archive, Miller also became an important technical witness, explaining the console's expansion bus, custom-chip implementation, video hardware, memory timing, and the add-on's history.
accomplishments: Took over the Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on after Larry Leske left DNA, completing working prototype hardware and moving the design toward production.
Supported the add-on with Jay Fenton at a Winter CES and during demonstrations for Bally distributors on the West Coast.
Requested the BUZOFF expansion-bus signal so external hardware could disconnect the custom-chip microcycle bus and return data to the Z80.
Helped design DNA's dedicated Z80 development-system probe with Terry Coleman.
Recruited former DNA engineers for Universal Research Laboratories and managed Stern's Berzerk development team.
Documented the Bally Professional Arcade's video and memory architecture for the preservation community and provided extensive firsthand technical corrections in the archive.
